analysis.one_liner: Repeals Depression-era limits on utility holding companies, replacing them with lighter federal record-keeping rules.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the 1935 Public Utility Holding Company Act was referred to two House subcommittees but never received a markup or vote, and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935, a New Deal law that required electric and gas holding companies to register with the Securities and Exchange Commission and restricted them to single, integrated utility systems. It would replace that regime with a much lighter one: federal and state regulators could demand records from holding company affiliates, but only for information relevant to utility rates, and FERC would have to exempt qualifying facilities, exempt wholesale generators, and foreign utility companies from the requirements [S2][S3]. The SEC's role would end entirely, with its files on utility holding companies transferred to FERC [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Large electric and gas utility holding companies and their shareholders. Repeal ends SEC registration and the 1935 Act's structural limits, freeing holding companies to diversify into non-utility businesses, acquire other companies, and expand beyond their historic service territories without federal approval. Independent power producers, exempt wholesale generators, and foreign utility companies gain further, since FERC must exempt them from even the records-access requirements [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large utility holding companies and their shareholders

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935 twelve months after enactment, ending SEC registration and oversight of utility holding companies and the structural limits that kept them within single integrated utility systems.

Replaces the old regime with a narrower one: FERC and state commissions get access to holding company books and records, but only to the extent the information is relevant to costs in jurisdictional utility rates.

Requires FERC to exempt qualifying facilities, exempt wholesale generators, and foreign utility companies from the records-access requirements within 90 days, and allows FERC to exempt any person or transaction it finds not relevant to jurisdictional rates.

Preserves FERC and state authority to decide whether a utility may recover the costs of affiliate transactions in rates, which the bill's findings present as sufficient consumer protection after repeal.

analysis.who_pays: Electric and gas ratepayers. They would keep rate regulation, but lose the 1935 Act's structural guardrails — SEC registration, limits on holding company structure, and restrictions on non-utility business — and would instead rely on after-the-fact records requests limited to rate-relevant information, with broad exemptions (including for foreign utility companies) and state access available only on written request for records identified in advance [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The replacement regime is much thinner than the law it repeals: state commissions can obtain records only on written request, for records 'identified in reasonable detail' in advance, and FERC can exempt any person or transaction it deems not relevant to jurisdictional rates — leaving regulators with a weaker tool to detect inflated affiliate costs buried anywhere in a sprawling corporate structure.

Foreign utility companies are exempt from the records-access requirements, meaning affiliates organized abroad could sit outside the reach of federal and state examiners even when their transactions feed into domestic utility rates.

A good-faith defense of the bill: the 1935 Act predated modern FERC and state rate regulation, and much of its SEC apparatus duplicated oversight those regulators already exercised over affiliate costs, so repeal could remove real compliance burden without touching the authority to set rates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades away the 1935 Act's structural protections — SEC registration, limits on holding company sprawl, and restrictions on non-utility business — in exchange for a records-access regime that applies only to jurisdictional rates and comes with mandatory exemptions for foreign utility companies and other categories. Rate regulation itself would continue, but the proactive, structural layer of oversight that existed to catch cross-subsidization before it reached customer bills would be gone, replaced by after-the-fact requests for documents regulators must first identify. The efficiency gains for holding companies are real; the added risk to ratepayers of harder-to-detect affiliate cost-shifting is also real, and the bill provides no new substantive safeguard to offset it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 1998 and sent to the House Commerce Committee, which passed it down to two subcommittees where it sat until the Congress ended — no markup, no vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Rep. W. J. (Billy) Tauzin of Louisiana introduced the bill on May 22, 1998, joined by ten original cosponsors including Rep. Joe Barton of Texas and Rep. Richard Burr-backed colleagues from both parties.
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce the same day it was introduced.
On June 5, 1998, the committee referred it to two subcommittees — Finance and Hazardous Materials, and Energy and Power — where it remained without any further action.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ratepayers kept the 1935 Act's structural protections intact for at least another Congress, since the repeal never advanced; utility holding companies and their investors, who had sought repeal, gained nothing from this attempt.

for.name: Rep. W. J. (Billy) Tauzin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 13 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including several members of the Energy and Commerce Committee.

for.name: House Energy and Power and Finance and Hazardous Materials subcommittees
for.role: Subcommittees of the House Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on June 5, 1998, and took no further action on it.

against.name: Rep. Thomas Bliley
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; the bill went no further than subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the sponsor and 10 of 13 cosponsors were Republicans, with 3 Democrats, so the bill skewed Republican but drew some bipartisan support without ever being tested.

industries.industry: Electric and gas utility holding companies
industries.note: Repeal would end SEC registration and the 1935 Act's structural limits, letting holding companies diversify into non-utility businesses, make acquisitions, and expand beyond their historic service territories without federal approval. Ratepayers would lose the structural guardrails against cross-subsidization and inflated affiliate transactions, relying instead on narrower after-the-fact rate reviews.

industries.industry: Independent power producers, exempt wholesale generators, and foreign utility investors
industries.note: The bill requires FERC to exempt qualifying facilities, exempt wholesale generators, and foreign utility companies from the records-access requirements, and lets FERC exempt anyone whose records it finds irrelevant to jurisdictional rates. Their interest in exemption runs against the transparency regulators would need to police costs that flow into customer rates.

industries.industry: Financial and securities firms seeking to invest in utilities
industries.note: Repealing the 1935 Act would open utility holding companies to acquisition and investment by any company or investor without SEC review. This lowers barriers to capital but also ends the screening that once limited who could control essential utility assets.
